speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC  DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take this opportunity to extend our best wishes to our French speaking friends at this time when they are all celebrating together their national holiday, the feast of St. John the Baptist.
This year, I know, their national holiday has been extended to exceptional proportions. The people of French Canada are celebrating their origins and asserting their identity during a whole week. This is all to their credit. It is proof positive of their dynamic strength, their vitality and their attachment to traditions.

In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this attachment to tradition is an important element in a country that wishes to progress, but with ease and stability, toward greatness. In our country an even more indispensable condition is the establishment of a spirit of unity among people of all races and all sections of our country so we can give the world an example of good will and mutual understanding. We think of this good will and understanding, Mr. Speaker, as we congratulate our French speaking colleagues in the house and our French speaking fellow Canadians on this, their special day.
The feast day of St. John the Baptist has an additional meaning in the history of Canada, for it was on this day 466 years ago that the redoubtable explorer John Cabot-or Jean Cabot or Giovanni Caboto, as you will- had the great fortune to discover the land that became the ancient colony and is now the Canadian province of Newfoundland, to which stalwart and courageous people we also pay our tribute of respect today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC  DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join
with the Prime Minister on this occasion and it gives me great pleasure to extend to all French speaking Canadians my heartfelt congratulations on this their national holiday, the feast of St. John the Baptist.

Sir, it is very seldom that the Prime Minister and I have the opportunity to reveal in such a striking manner our capacity to express ourselves in the French language. This is an occasion not only for those who are French Canadians but for all of us to pause in solemn recollection of the splendid contribution they have made to Canada. It is an occasion on which we share the memory of that faith that made possible the preservation of this portion of the North American continent under the British crown, and the contribution since which continues to grow and expand. It is well to recall on an occasion such as this that in 1864, none other than Sir George Etienne Cartier, speaking on behalf of those of French origin, said that without confederation the result would be the absorption, progressive and inevitable, of Canada into the American orbit as part of the United States of America. Whether overtly through formal recognition or not, there would have been absorption in fact, economically, socially and culturally but for the confederation that binds us. We on this occasion join with our compatriots of the French race and language and bid for them an equal partnership which is essential to the preservation of the unity of our country.
The Prime Minister mentioned as well the fact that this is Newfoundland Discovery day. This reminded me of the fact that over that long period of time since John Cabot made his discovery the union jack has floated over that country, whether as a colony or as a province. We join on this day in paying our tribute to those from Newfoundland who today, having joined us, are making their contribution to the unity of our country which was the hope of the fathers of confederation and which was not achieved until more than 80 years thereafter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I visited the dentist and he told me that he had succeeded in preventing me from speaking for at least 48

St. John the Baptist Day hours. I regret to say he has been only partially successful. However, I shall have sufficient difficulty in saying anything in English without trying to mangle the French language at this particular time.
I do want, on behalf of the New Democratic party, to join with those who have spoken in extending our congratulations to our French Canadian colleagues in this house and our French Canadian compatriots across Canada in this celebration of St. John the Baptist day. We rejoice in the pride which they take in their culture and traditions. I am sure that all of us were inspired this week by the words of Cardinal Leger in which he set forth, in moderate terms and with far-seeing vision, the hope that the French people and English people would work out the necessary modus vivendi to build here in Canada a great country.
We join with all those who on this day are celebrating the feast day of the French Canadian patron saint. We trust that their pride in their race, their language and their culture will have every reason to continue to grow from year to year.

maintopic: ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC  DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure, on behalf of the members of our group-particularly those from the province of Quebec-and in the name of all my fellow countrymen, to sincerely thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) for the feelings they expressed toward all French Canadians on this occasion of the feast of St. John the Baptist, patron saint of French Canadians from Quebec and all other provinces in Canada.
All French Canadians, throughout Canada, are celebrating today the feast of their patron saint. Of course, those celebrations are specially prominent in the province of Quebec and this year it was the intent of the organizers of this feast day, all across Quebec, that it be even more imposing through diversified celebrations which got under way last Saturday and will be going on until next Saturday, while reaching their peak this evening. Such an exceptional pageant on this occasion is a mark of a sound vitality within the French-Canadian people who, more than ever, are conscious of the role they must and can play and of the importance of their contribution in the development and the establishment of
[Mr. Douglas.)
a Canada strong and united in the diversity of its parts.
The magnitude of today's celebrations in Quebec must in no way be interpreted as a sign of hostility toward anyone or anything.
It is only the evidence of our will to contribute to the making of Canada, my country, our country, a place where it will be good to live together harmoniously.
But, in order to achieve that harmony as soon as possible, we must show on both sides some understanding and moderation.

Mr. Speaker, now that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have spoken a few words in French I would like to attempt to say something in English. I would like to quote from an editorial in today's Montreal Gazette to bring to the attention of the house what it said about French Canada and about this particular day:
The vigour of French Canada today is the vigour of a society seeking a new and progressive identity. And if this vigour sometimes seems to have about it a great hunger, this is not surprising.
It went on to say:
During the past few years, there have been some, including some of marked talent, who have followed paths of extremism. But the over-all movement of French Canada has been one of positive and purposeful advance. Every French Canadian, and every friend of French Canada, can take pride in what has been done.
This year the spirit of St. John the Baptist day is one of confidence. It is a spirit that is fully justified. For this is the spirit of French Canada today. The paths of progress are open. And French Canadians are following them as never before in their history.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make these words mine, and I would like to have it that Canada will be strong if Quebec, where one third of all Canadians live, is strong, and that is how sincere Quebeckers wish it. I would also like to extend my sincere congratulations to our fellow Canadians from Newfoundland and say that we share with them this particular day, June 24, as one of the most important days for the people of Quebec and Newfoundland. I also hope that, as the years go round, St. John the Baptist will become the patron saint of all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of our group, on behalf of all hon. members-and I think that unanimity is not a problem on that matter-as well as on behalf of all French Canadians, we wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the leader of the official

opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and others who expressed their best wishes to the French Canadians on the occasion of our national holiday.
This year the celebrations are on a larger scale than usual and express our nation's maturity. A sculpture wrought in solid metal, has replaced the sheep to show our solidity, our vitality and our energy.
Mr. Speaker, the French Canadian nation will live on because it has faith in its future. We are confident that we have made to Canada and North America a vast cultural contribution which can only benefit all the citizens of this continent.
Our two great cultures existing side by side in Canada are the patent evidence that we can make of our country a powerful country where the true human values, the cultural values will be put in the foreground, making of Canada a still greater country because it will have as a basis the greatest of all values, culture.

I should like to take this opportunity to invite all members of this house to the celebration of St. John the Baptist day in Montreal so that each and every one of them may be able to see for themselves what is going on in French Canada today. They will see, amid all the demonstrations and parades tonight, that French Canada is full of life and is ready to contribute to the development of a great and powerful country, Canada.

subtopic: DUMPING OF RAW SEWAGE INTO GREAT LAKES
DUMPING OF RAW SEWAGE INTO GREAT LAKES
speechtext: In connection with the strong recommendation by the international joint commission to cease dumping raw sewage and other waste products in the great lakes system (a) what program has been decided on in Canada to this end (b) how many American and Canadian communities dump raw sewage, directly or indirectly, into the great lakes system (c) have the American people assumed any time limit on any program to clean up the water in the great lakes system by sewage disposal plants, elimination of detergents and other wastes etc.?

subtopic: DUMPING OF RAW SEWAGE INTO GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
(a) The I.J.C.
program relates only to the connecting channels of the great lakes where surveillance of water quality is actively maintained by the commission's technical advisory board.
In Ontario, jurisdiction over matters relating to water pollution abatement rests with the Ontario water resources commission, which, under its act, has the power to control and regulate the collection, production, treatment, storage, transmission, distribution and use of water for public purposes and to make orders with respect thereto. The commission maintains an energetic and effective program which includes a constant review of those municipalities and industries which are deficient in the provision of waste treatment facilities.
Pollution of Canadian waters by oil from vessels is covered by the oil pollution prevention regulations under the Canada Shipping Act. The question of providing appropriate regulations covering other waste from vessels is presently being studied.
(b)	At the present time, ten Canadian communities having a total population of 232,850, discharge untreated or insufficiently treated sewage into the great lakes. Similar information regarding U.S. communities has been requested from the U.S. authorities and will be provided as soon as available.
(c)	Information is being requested from the U.S. authorities and will be provided when available.

speechtext:
1.	What charges, If any, existed against Hooper during the time he was incarcerated in jail for 90 to 100 days, other than the fact that he was held in custody for refusing to answer certain questions alleged to be in accordance with the regulations and law?
2.	How many times during the 90 to 100 days of Hooper's incarceration was he brought before the court for a further remand in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Criminal Code of Canada?
3.	During the 90 to 100 days that the said Hooper was incarcerated before being deported, how many times was he questioned by those in authority or by the court as to whether he was willing to answer the questions which it was alleged he refused to so answer?
4.	How many people are at the present time incarcerated in Canada under similar conditions that Mr. Hooper was held?
5.	How many people were held during the period of 90 to 100 days the said Hooper was held?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: DETENTION AWAITING
speechtext:
1. Harry Claude Hooper came under the jurisdiction of the Immigration Act on March 16, 1964. Prior to that time his detention was the responsibility of local police. He was detained from March 16 to May 26, 1964, a total of 71 days. He was detained from March 16 to March 23 to enable him to obtain counsel if he so wished at an immigration inquiry. Because he refused to answer any questions, the inquiry was adjourned from March 23 to April 7 to obtain essential documentary evidence that he was deportable and from April 7 to May 26 he was detained pending completion of travel arrangements and deportation. On May 22 he was charged under section 50(e) of the Immigration Act for having refused to answer questions. Section 50(e) of the act reads as follows:
Every person who refuses to be sworn or to affirm or declare, as the case may be, or to answer a question put to him or does not truthfully answer all questions put to him at an examination or inquiry under this act is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction, for the first offence to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and not less than one month or to both fine and imprisonment, and, for the second offence to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars and not less than one hundred dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding twelve months and not less than three months or to both fine and imprisonment, and, for the third or a subsequent offence to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 18 months and not less than six months.
Questions
This charge was withdrawn on May 26 and Hooper was deported May 26.
2.	Subsequent to March 16, 1964, Hooper appeared before an immigration inquiry on March 23 and April 7. He was charged in court on May 22. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MEETING OF JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is to be a meeting tomorrow. It is a regular meeting of the

ministerial defence committee of Canada and the United States such as has been held in the past. The Canadian government will be represented by the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Defence Production, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

maintopic: MEETING OF JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. maintopic: MEETING OF JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE

subtopic: HUNGARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is intended for the Secretary of State for External Affairs but in his absence perhaps I can address it to his parliamentary secretary. What steps are being taken to assist a Canadian citizen by the name of Christian Reuter, who is reported to have been arrested and held by the Hungarian authorities? This matter takes on particular significance since only in the last few days it has been announced that diplomatic relations have been established between the two countries.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: HUNGARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some information on that matter, and perhaps my hon. friend would permit me to answer for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Christian Reuter's plight, I am informed, was reported last week by the Canadian embassy in Vienna. There is no Canadian representative in Budapest; therefore the British embassy there kindly consented to act on our behalf. Accordingly the British consul applied to the Hungarian authorities seeking the right of consular access to Mr. Reuter in order that the circumstances of his arrest might be established, his treatment investigated and his rights as a Canadian citizen upheld. Up to this moment the British consul has not yet been granted consular access, and it is therefore not possible to provide the house with the official facts concerning Mr. Reuter's arrest, detention and the nature of the charge. I can assure the house and the hon. member that every effort is being made on his behalf.

maintopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF PRICES PAID BY LIVESTOCK FEEDERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Maurice Sauve (Minister of Forestry) moved:
maintopic: COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF PRICES PAID BY LIVESTOCK FEEDERS
speechtext: That the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to examine and inquire forthwith into all matters arising out of and relating to the difference between the prices received for feed grain by the producers in the prairie provinces of Canada and the price paid by livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia, and that the evidence adduced before this committee in the twenty sixth parliament be referred to the committee, and that the committee have leave to receive such evidence as part of the said examination.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps the committee would expect the chairman at this time to express an opinion or render a judgment in connection with the very important point of order which was raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs shortly before we adjourned last evening. The minister at that time took exception to and requested a ruling from the Chair concerning certain expressions used by the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Yukon.
The minister said, as reported at page 4644 of yesterday's Hansard:
-the hon. gentleman cannot under the rules of this house be allowed to go unchallenged when he suggests that the Prime Minister has misinformed this house-
And later, as recorded at page 4645 of Hansard the minister said:
I ask you, sir, to ask the hon. gentleman who spoke just before the hon. member for Yukon to withdraw what he said about the statement made by the Prime Minister, and the hon. member for Yukon a moment ago has violated our rules when he referred to statements made by the Prime Minister as lies.
Referring first to the words used by the hon. member for Bow River, these words are reported at page 4644 of yesterday's Hansard. The hon. member said:
None of us saw him rise in his place, Mr. Chairman, to answer the charge that he had misinformed the house.
These are the words to which the minister took exception, and I must say in my opinion the suggestion that there is misinforming of the house is not unparliamentary. I believe this statement or this phrase would have to be coupled with the suggestion that the misinforming was deliberate and voluntary to make it a breach of the privileges of the house and to make the phrase unparliamentary. This is my ruling in connection with that point.
Now, I would like to refer to the other matter referred to in the point of order raised by the minister. This has reference to the statements made by the hon. member for

Interim Supply
Yukon, and these are reported at page 4645 of yesterday's Hansard where the hon. member for Yukon said:
I said, sir, concerning those words quoted, that they were lies and I maintain they were lies-
I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that those words constituted rather strong language and my impression, knowing the hon. gentleman, was that perhaps they were uttered in the heat of debate and went beyond his thoughts. I would ask the hon. member if he would, perhaps, rephrase the statement he has made in order to facilitate the position of the Chair.

I want to be as co-operative as possible in all the circumstances. I think it would be rather difficult to rephrase, as Your Honour has suggested, the words I used last night. But before entering upon the merits of the point raised by Your Honour I wish to draw your attention to a point of order which the Chair may have overlooked and which may have been overlooked also by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
If Your Honour would refer to page 121 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, 1958, and page 120, citation 138(2) you will see there is a specific procedure set out which must be adopted in committee and by the Speaker of the house in order to set the wheels in motion, should there be any question of enforcing an order which might be made by Your Honour or by Mr. Speaker. This procedure is also set out in May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, commencing at page 468. The substance of these rules-I do not intend to go into detail now, but if the matter is pursued I should like to reserve the right to deal with it in more detail-the substance appears to be, according to May at page 473, that the matter must be raised at once, and if the house is in committee a specific procedure is laid down whereby the Chairman reports to the Speaker, and thus begins the chain of procedure which must then be followed. I raise this point now because I feel the point of order takes precedence over the suggestion made by Your Honour that the words I made last night should be altered in any way at all.
In brief, my statement at this time is that the matter must be dealt with at once and, therefore, that there is no jurisdiction resting with Your Honour or with Mr. Speaker to deal with it now at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not wish to argue with the hon. member but he must realize that when we had to adjourn at ten o'clock the
[The Chairman.)
matter was then under consideration, and we are now continuing the consideration of the matter which was under way at that time. It is true that an objection must be made immediately if any member objects to words uttered by hon. members in committee, in the same way as objection must be taken in the house. But this, to my mind, is exactly what the minister did. These words were uttered as reported at page 4645 by the hon. member for Yukon. He said he had uttered those words, and he repeated them. He said: "I maintain they were lies". This is the moment when the Secretary of State for External Affairs raised the point, and I do not agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Yukon that it was too late then, or that it is too late now, to pursue the matter.
On this particular question of procedure I must rule against the hon. member and I again ask him to give serious thought to withdrawing the words he used.

Well, I only wish at this time, before the procedure develops further, to refer Your Honour to page 4630 of Hansard where, in the right hand column, in addition to the words quoted subsequently by Your Honour from Hansard, I said, as reported: "I am not going to say that the Prime Minister lied."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not wish to put the hon. member in a difficult position, but he has just confirmed what I said. When he made that statement as reported at page 4630 he could not be called to order because he did not make a statement that these were lies. But he did make a statement, as reported at page 4645, and these were his words- unless they were incorrectly reported in Hansard and, if they were, now is the time to make the correction; he used the words: "I maintain they were lies". Perhaps the hon. member would like to tell us that he was wrong when he said what was reported at page 4645, and that what he really believes is what he said as recorded on page 4630 of Hansard.

I can only repeat that as reported at page 4630 of Hansard, I said: "I am not going to say that the Prime Minister lied". But when we read page 3429 of Hansard we find the following answer given by the Prime Minister to a question: "We do not censor films on this side of the house". I say, sir, that that is a lie, because that is precisely what happened. I would point out, too, that at page 3430 of Hansard we find

a reply by the Prime Minister which is reported as follows:
The circumstances were perfectly proper. The initiative was taken by the producer of the film, and no question of censorship arises.
I also say that that statement is a lie. I went on to say, as reported at the page Your Honour has mentioned, page 4645-to quote the words in their full context:
If the minister will stop his attempts at closure I will complete my point of order. I said, sir, concerning those words I quoted, that they were lies and I maintain that they were lies.
That, in my humble opinion, sir, is my view of the matter. There was a question of censorship involved. That is what the whole debate is about, and this question of censorship has been under debate now for two days, as well as during several question periods; it concerns the statement by the Prime Minister that there was no censorship on that side of the house. This whole debate revolves around the matter of government censorship and, in my humble view, the statement that there is no censorship involved in this question is as I described it.
I suggest we accept the hon. gentleman's explanation as satisfactory and sufficient.
No martyrs today.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, the matter rests with the committee, and if the Prime Minister, who is actually the person concerned, accepts the words which have just been spoken by the hon. member for Yukon I have no further quarrel and I will recognize the hon. member for Bow River.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I might-
My hon. friend from Bow River had the floor. Ordinarily, I do not raise these matters, but it seems to me-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is correct. The hon. member for Bow River had the floor last night and should be allowed to conclude his remarks.

I shall be very brief. I began to answer an attack upon me with reference to remarks I made earlier in the evening; I felt duty bound to answer those remarks.
In brief, I was accused of making a vicious attack upon the Prime Minister. This was said by the hon. member for Verdun. I was accused of making an unwarranted attack upon him. I was accused of making a preinterim Supply
meditated attack upon him. If to point out
to members of this house and to the country facts in absolute contradiction to the statements of the Prime Minister-if that is what the hon. member means by "vicious", then I am guilty. If it is unwarranted for me to dare to bring forward definite, concise contradictions made by the Prime Minister of this country when we on this side of the house are seeking information-if that is what the hon. member for Verdun meant by "unwarranted", I am guilty. If, in the words of the hon. member for Verdun, I have prostituted my ability clearly to bring before the house the facts relating to the C.B.C. and to other matters, but particularly relating to the C.B.C. to keep it independent politically, to keep it free from bias and to keep it out of the field of politics-and I did this with all the ability I can command-if that is what he means by that statement, then I am guilty. I say I am guilty because it is my responsibility to the people I represent, as it is also the responsibility of us all to the people of the nation and to parliament, to bring these facts carefully before parliament in relation to any other member, particularly in relation to the Prime Minister of this country. If by a "premeditated attack" the hon. member meant that I had done some research, read through Hansard and picked out those absolute contradictions, if that is the charge he makes against me, then I am guilty.
However, if the charge he made against me, which I say he failed to prove, was that I took out of context statements in Hansard or statements made in the debate itself, then I am innocent. I have appeared, and I say this with modesty, in every court in Canada, including this court, which is the highest court in the land, and I have never been accused of taking anything out of context, either unintentionally, as in the argument I produced yesterday, or intentionally. In that regard I say I am innocent. No words that Mr. Kent or anyone else wishes to place in the hands of the hon. member will create such fear that I will shirk my responsibility first to my constituency, then to the nation and to every hon. member in this house. Good or bad press is immaterial when one is dealing with the facts in this house. The facts must be known.
The hon. member for Verdun, speaking for the cabinet as their agent-and he admitted that to me very frankly-stated that in this day and age people of the stature of the Prime Minister of Canada should never be

Interim Supply
subjected to that kind of attack. I say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the hon. member who does not appear to be in the committee this afternoon-
Yes he is.

I am sorry; I did not see him. I would say to him this, that I intend,
and I accept this as my responsibility, to bring these facts before the house. But if he thinks that this kind of attack was a vicious attack or was an unwarranted attack I should like to call a very good witness before the bar of the House of Commons. This witness of whom I speak gave on September 18, 1962, the evidence I will produce. If that distinguished member used the kind of language he used at that time with reference to another prime minister, I would have thought that the hon. member for Verdun should carefully analyse his remarks when he charges that I made an unwarranted attack on the Prime Minister.
It seems very strange, Mr. Chairman, that these men who now sit on the cabinet benches and who used to sit on this side in the past could make the kind of personal attacks that they did make in the past, and it would be all right. But this is the new era. This is the era of 60 days; this is the era of decision. And what decision. Today, because they sit on that side of the house, if people bring forward the facts in parliament for the people of Canada to read and appreciate, this is unwarranted and vicious.
Now let us see what this distinguished witness said on this former occasion. I observe some hon. members on the other side of the house are starting to wriggle because they do not know which witness I am going to call to the bar of this house. This witness can be corroborated in this kind of conduct by many who now sit in high places. This speech was made on September 18, 1962 by the present Prime Minister in Toronto when he was addressing the district Liberal members of parliament in the Royal York hotel. In these references he was referring to the present Leader of the Opposition. So that we get the atmosphere of this speech, it was made after the 1962 election, after the charge by the Liberals, who were then in opposition, with reference to the financial situation-and I see the minister of health trying to say something. Anyway, I could bring her in as a good witness if she wants.
In this speech these are some of the things the present Prime Minister said against the

then prime minister. At that time no one now on that side said it was unwarranted, no one said it was vicious. Oh no-it was good for the country, because hon. members opposite were hungry for power. First of all the right hon. gentleman was very mild in tone. He said it was an "incredible effrontery," referring to the then prime minister. Then in dealing with the financial problem which arose during the election and the explanation given by the then prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, he said it was "gross and unpardonable deceit", still referring to the then prime minister. Then he referred to another man who was recently expelled from this house because he dared stand up in his place and bring certain facts before the house. This is what he said of him on that occasion, that "he still kept up the deceit". That is referring to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
On the second page of his speech the Prime Minister said this about the then prime minister:
The prime minister, after the election was over, did not try any longer to conceal the facts.
In other words, the present Prime Minister charged the then prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, with concealing facts. If I were to use that kind of language this afternoon, or if I had used that kind of language yesterday, I would be called to order. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is not here this afternoon, would have risen from his seat. Today he is out of the atmosphere of politics; but yesterday he would have said that it was terrible for anyone to use that kind of language. And particularly so, said the hon. member for Verdun, against the Prime Minister of the country. 1 say with the greatest respect to the Prime Minister, to his person and to his position that in the House of Commons in debate we recognize the Prime Minister as the leader of the country and the leader of the house. But, as the former president of the United States, Harry Truman, said, if in debate you cannot stand the heat, stay out of the kitchen.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He stayed out last night.

I will now move on to page 3 of this speech. He said that it was a "farcical explanation" and that there was "contempt of parliament". Then he went on to say that the former prime minister was-
-the man who cannot make a speech without boasting how he has restored the rights of parliament.

Then he referred to all of the Conservative cabinet and put them in the same category, every one of them. This is what he said about them. He referred to "the government's stupidity and deceit"-he used the word "deceit". We know, Mr. Chairman, what the word "deceit" means. It means deliberate deception, in this case of the people, the House of Commons and the members of the House of Commons.
I now come back to my original point. When I made my attack yesterday afternoon, which I felt I did with responsibility and justification, the great brains of the Liberal party handed down a speech, which was read here, which said in effect that I had prostituted my ability and that I had made an unwarranted and a vicious attack. Why was that said? It was because the government realized that this attack was justified, and if they could whitewash the news items in the press of this country to make it more mild and palatable the people might accept it and understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Everyone is against you.
I hear the minister of health saying they are all against me. After seeing certain cartoons which went across the land I do not think she should talk like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a matter of personal privilege. May I suggest to my hon. friend that if he is desirous of appearing in cartoons I would be pleased to present him to several members of the press gallery.

I do not want to get into an argument at the moment with the minister of health, but I was thinking about that last cartoon I saw where the present Prime Minister was walking up the staircase with two balls and chains, one representing the minister of health and the other the Minister of Finance. That may have been the reason why when I raised my first question of privilege on this matter, the Prime Minister blushed and looked as red as a beet. If hon. members opposite care to read what the present Prime Minister said in that same speech, they will see that he linked Mr. Diefenbaker with the London Daily Worker; he linked Mr. Diefenbaker with Khrushchev, with regard to the suggestion concerning a world trade conference. In other words, it was fine for the Prime Minister, then the leader of the opposition, to call a then Conservative prime minister deceitful; it was fine for him to link the prime minister with the Daily Worker; it was fine for him to link the then prime minister with Khrushchev-and it was also fine for 20220-297
Interim Supply
any man who sat in high places to refer to him as a nazi.
That was the kind of abuse that poured out across this nation for five years. Sometimes we Tories have to take off our coats, because this is an old, Liberal trick, namely that in order to defeat a Conservative government the first thing you do is destroy its leader. They did it to Arthur Meighen; they did it to Bracken; they did it to Drew, and they did it to E. B. Bennett from my own city- and they finally tried to do it to the present Leader of the Opposition. But they have not succeeded.
Hear, hear.

So they hired a boy to do a man's job last night, because these people over there on the front benches were not in the chamber at the time. I want to hear from the cabinet on this; I want an explanation of these matters; I want to hear what they have to say.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman.
We could put on-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Verdun is rising on a question of privilege.

Is he rising because he isn't
a boy?

Mr. Chairman, I would accept that description of myself in preference to the one the hon. member used last evening on a question of privilege. I had no intention of interrupting the hon. member, but on several occasions in his speech so far he has emphasized that someone else wrote my speech for me. I know it may be straining the credulity of the hon. member, but I would ask him to accept as a fact that I prepared my own speech, as I have always prepared my speeches, whether they have been ordinary or excellent, in my short political career. Whether the hon. member accepts that fact or not is entirely up to him. While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, I may say that I completely accept-I say this in the presence of everybody-the hon. member's admission of guilt as he eloquently expressed it at the beginning of his remarks.

Well, Mr. Chairman, if the
hon. member said he did write that speech, there is one thing we are sure of-that he did read that speech.

Shame.

Interim Supply
Somebody said "shame". Of course it is a shame; it takes up the time of the house and it is so uninteresting.
Not as uninteresting as your speech.

Before I leave this matter, Mr. Chairman, I want to put a little more evidence on the record. I wish to read from Hansard of May 21, page 3428. This is in reference to a communication with Her Majesty the Queen with respect to the flag. This is what the Prime Minister said about this particular matter. There are dozens of these cases that I could mention, but I want to put one more on the record:
Perhaps that will explain the inaccuracy of the right hon. gentleman's report.

Is the report inaccurate in stating that the Prime Minister said that he had telegraphed the Queen and had advised her that the red ensign would not be our flag?
This is the point:

Yes, it is inaccurate.
Meaning that he had not telegraphed the Queen. A few days passed, not very many; and just so we have the record straight I would point out that this was on Thursday. Then there was Friday, Saturday, Sunday; and on Monday-
Jack returned.
Yes, Jack returned. I should now like to read from Hansard of May 25, 1964, page 3533:

Mr. Speaker, I think I should tell the house that I have, in an informal way, informed the Queen, through her private secretary, of the intentions of the government in this matter, without of course asking for the Queen's advice, which would he unconstitutional. As a matter of courtesy it was surely desirable to let the Queen know what the intentions of the government were in this matter, and that has been done.
Why didn't you tell the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) ?

Mr. Speaker, I do not want the Prime Minister in any way to go into detail, because the Queen would not get any more information than the house has received, I suppose-
Then there is this passage:
-but would the Prime Minister say when it was that he communicated with the secretary of Her Majesty the Queen?
I ask hon. members to keep in mind that the Prime Minister said he had not communicated with Her Majesty the Queen, and to keep in mind that the Prime Minister does not contact the Queen directly.
Oh, oh.

You can't shout me down now; you can make as much noise as you want. I know you don't like to hear these facts because you feel very uncomfortable; and I know the Prime Minister will be blushing today as he did when he refused to answer the question of privilege.
We would like to have facts, not fiction.
I never knew the debates in Hansard were fiction, except when the hon. member who has interrupted me is talking.
It is your interpretation that is fiction.
I will continue reading from Hansard:
-but would the Prime Minister say when it was that he communicated with the secretary of Her Majesty the Queen?

I have not the exact date in my mind, Mr. Speaker.
Not the exact date. Then he said:
The first communication was a good many days ago, and there has been one since that time.
In the house on Thursday the Prime Minister said there was no communication, and on Monday he said there was communication.
No.

My friends say no. We are anxious to hear the explanations of these things.
I now want to turn to one other subject before I sit down, Mr. Chairman. I think it is very important because we do not want to lose the perspective of the debate. First of all, these irregularities and contradictions were pointed out because we have read in the newspapers recently and have heard a lot of talk about the respect for parliament; but if members of the opposition cannot get the information for which they ask, if they cannot get the information without wishy-washy answers or contradictory answers, respect for parliament will go down and down, and not only will we lose our democratic system but we will eventually lose parliament itself.
Let us consider the C.B.C. for a few moments. I need not remind hon. members that the C.B.C. was incorporated as an independent corporation. It is supposed to be independent from political influence; it is supposed to be away from bias. But I say this to the Prime Minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that the way they have conducted this affair over the famous Pearson film raises a great many queries in our minds. It is not

the $35,000 the taxpayers have thrown in the wastepaper basket that we are complaining about; but as soon as they get into the realm of communications it is a sad state of affairs, because we know what has happened in other lands when any government has controlled thought by communication.
I say they have politically interfered with the C.B.C. If we could have certain members of the C.B.C. appear before a special committee, when it would not be said that heads would roll in the aisle and they could come here freely, to a free institution and speak for themselves, they would say how many calls they have received from the Prime Minister's office on this and other matters; they would say how much interference there has been from other cabinet members. The C.B.C. was incorporated as an independent body to be a news medium and means of communication across this nation.
Hear, hear.

My good friends clap; they make noises, but their words do not bear out the purpose for which the C.B.C. was incorporated. They have interfered with the C.B.C.; they are guilty of censorship and interference. I still say that I hoped that on the day I raised the question of privilege, yesterday, there would have been a few more cabinet members in the chamber. At one time we were down to eight or nine members on that side. It was a serious charge. I made it with responsibility and I made it because I believed it was my duty to the people of my constituency, the people of the nation and to the members of parliament in this house.

Mr. Chairman, I greatly welcome the opportunity to take part in this discussion and in doing so I do not propose to go back and read the election speeches or post-election speeches of leading members of the opposition. I propose to confine my remarks to what has been happening in the house as appears in Hansard. I have made the same kind of election speech which my hon. friend who has just sat down complains so bitterly about when they are uttered by members on this side of the house, and no doubt in the heat of debate outside the house at political meetings we do say things which we should perhaps regret later. At times we may even accuse members of this house of being more interested in their salary increase than they are in the settling of the flag question.
Interim Supply
The hon. member who just sat down once said, and I am sure he regrets this very much, that the Liberal party is a cesspool of civil servants with red friends.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. What I did say at the time Hazen Argue, who had said he was a socialist, joined the Liberal party was that birds of a feather flock together and birds of red feathers roost together.

Yes, we have the hon. member's speech, and he also said that. But this is a kind of idle talk. What we want to do is decide in respect of the situation which is now before us on the basis of the facts because the facts, Mr. Chairman, often give a sufficient answer to the product of frenzied imaginations or calculated malevolence.
I am sorry that I was not able to be in the house last night to listen to what was apparently a very interesting evening of debate. In my present office there are certain duties and obligations which keep me out of the house. They entail certain sacrifices and my absence last night was one of those sacrifices. The extent and nature of the sacrifice I will leave to those who were here and were subjected to the debate.
I do not want to spend very much time dealing with the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River, but I want to thank him for his reiterated respect for the office of the prime minister, uttered with a kind of nauseating sanctimoniousness, very often as a prelude, to use his own words, to taking off his coat and destroying the leader. I also want to thank him for his devotion to the standards of parliamentary purity and the dignity and decency of debate. These are things we can all support, however inadequate we may be in our performance.
But I have to refer to what he said because he has demanded my resignation. This is a very serious matter, Mr. Chairman.
Let us have it.

He has demanded my resignation, not on the ground that I produced an economic report marked "confidential" with the page marked "confidential" torn off, not on the ground that I introduced into Hansard a forged letter designed to stir up trouble between Canada and the United States. The hon. gentleman, with his passion for the purity of parliament, was strangely silent when these things were done in the House

Interim Supply
of Commons. But now he thinks I should resign because I got a little mixed up about a meeting-
Oh, oh.
Oh, you got a little mixed up.

-concerning the Banff games that was held at the winter games in Austria, and perhaps I called a "conference" a "meeting" or something of that kind, that took place in Austria. I may have misled the house in relation to the nature of that meeting at Salzburg and I really do apologize. I should have said Innsbruck. There is another example of misleading the house. I said Salzburg when it was Innsbruck, but I really feel I cannot resign on those grounds.
Far more serious is the use I made or did not make of a letter from 12 intellectuals-
Sneeringly.
-dealing with the flag. The hon. gentleman opposite said I should resign because I misled the house by saying this letter was not signed, when it was signed. That is what he said.
I wonder whether the Prime Minister would read what I said.
I will deal with that.
Read it.

I received two letters, one addressed "Dear Mr. Prime Minister" and one addressed "Dear Mr. .. ". The "Dear Mr. .. " letter apparently was a kind of form letter reproduction of the first letter which was sent to a great many people, including members of parliament. It was sent to them by one of the 12, if not all 12, before I received the letter which was addressed to me. It had no address on the top and no salutation. I did get one about the same time-a little later, I think, because it was sent special delivery, and it was addressed "Dear Mr. Prime Minister". It had no indication of origin. It had no signature of any kind, except 12 typewritten names-not one signature, just 12 typewritten names, and no indication where I should send an acknowledgement if I desired to send one, as I generally do to my communications. There were just 12 typewritten names. We have to be very careful in receiving letters of this kind without signature, Mr. Chairman, because they might well be forged, and we on this side try to be careful about that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are still worried about that.
But the hon. member for Bow River has misled the house by stating this letter to me was signed.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. Would the Prime Minister read from Hansard where I said it was signed?

We will find it and I will be glad to read it. Here it is: "A signed communication", he said, "with 12 typewritten names". If the hon. gentleman has misled the house in this regard I hope he will at least resign his seat in accordance with his own precepts of divine and natural justice.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with this question of the film which has got me so much undeserved publicity. If and when it is shown, I think I am now guaranteed the largest audience that any Canadian television performer has had, including the hon. member for Port Arthur. For that, of course, I should be, and indeed I am, grateful. No doubt a decision is now being made by the C.B.C. board of directors as to whether or not I am to get this publicity.
Before I deal with certain aspects of the film, I want to clear up one point, I hope once and for all, although I am not quite sure my ambitions in that regard will be realized. I have been accused, as the leader of the government, of permitting cameramen into a meeting of the cabinet or a meeting of a cabinet committee. I confess, Mr. Speaker, I was very angry and indignant at that charge, even by implication, because that would have been a violation of my oath as a privy councillor. If indeed that had happened, I should resign. But it did not happen and the insinuations and suggestions that it did happen are false, misleading and untrue. There was no filming of a cabinet meeting or any part of a cabinet meeting or any committee of the cabinet. A picture was given to the press-by whom I do not know, presumably it would appear to be Intervideo Productions-of what purported to be a cabinet meeting, and was so described in certain newspapers where that picture appeared.
This picture, Mr. Chairman, was not of the cabinet in session which would, as I have said, have been a violation of our oath as privy councillors. Moreover, this picture did not appear, in fact, in the film as shown to the press, as the hon. member for Port Arthur must have known because he was

there, but who did not attempt to clarify the matter when it came up. The picture was in fact, Mr. Chairman, a shot of certain cabinet ministers in the cabinet room before a meeting. What was in the film, as shown to the press, I have ascertained from those who were there, was a discussion in my office with three or four ministers, the sort of thing I have every day and which the producer asked leave to photograph under conditions which I will refer to later. It was not a cabinet committee meeting. A cabinet committee has a formal agenda and formal minutes. What was photographed and included in the film was simply a sort of informal discussion with ministers in my office, such as take place practically every day.
There is of course, Mr. Chairman, no impropriety of any kind in taking a picture of the full cabinet before a meeting of the cabinet, in informal discussion. There is no impropriety in that procedure at any time. I have no doubt that when my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition was in office such a picture or pictures may have been taken and displayed in the press, pictures of cabinet ministers in discussion before a cabinet meeting occurred. I have no doubt in the world that that happened. Indeed there is no doubt on the point, so I hope there will not be any allegations of impropriety in using that picture.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about this famous but unseen film, its origin and its present position. I am very glad to have the opportunity of putting these facts on the record. This is the first opportunity I have had because it is not possible to tell the story in answer to questions. There has been no other opportunity. There was no other opportunity until we got into interim supply, and interim supply has been going on for two or three days. Naturally, I wished to hear the allegations and charges made by the other side before I stated what, in fact, had happened. If I had done otherwise, it is quite obvious what would have been the reaction of hon. gentlemen opposite. They would have said that while they were ambitious to get ahead with the flag resolution and the important legislation before this house, I had introduced this question into supply by making the first statement about it; that would have been the charge.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not answering statements made in the house by frontbenchers of the opposition. I am dealing with statements made by other members of the official opposition, and with questions that
Interim Supply
were raised on orders of the day. It is difficult to answer questions on a matter of this kind on orders of the day. If you give a simple, direct answer to the specific question asked, in its limited interpretation, you are accused of not telling the whole story. If you try to tell the whole story, the antecedents, surroundings, and so on, you are accused of trying to mislead the house by a wealth of detail. I have the opportunity now, Mr. Chairman, and I propose to take full advantage of it.
The idea of this film was first suggested to a member of my office in September, 1963, by a telephone call from a producer of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This telephone call was followed by a letter on September 9. I have a copy of that letter before me dated September 9. It is signed by Mr. Ross McLean, who is a producer for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and it is addressed to Mr. Richard O'Hagan, office of the Prime Minister, Ottawa, Ontario. This letter says this, he having made the request that we allow this to be done on behalf of the C.B.C.:
I know that you understand what such a request involves. I won't pretend that a film of this kind can be made without some intrusion into private areas of an individual's life. For a full understanding of the job he performs, we would need to follow him fairly closely over a period of several days. We would want to see him in a variety of official activities, and we would hope as well to see him informally at home and elsewhere.
He made a very strong plea that we allow this film to go on. I mention this because it is important, Mr. Chairman. It shows that the initiative in this matter, and this is important, did not come from anyone connected with my office or with the government; so there was no question of any image making overtures from the government which so upset the former minister of agriculture the other day. He thought we had been going in for image making, and this was the most horrible example he had yet discovered of this process. I welcome his conversion to the iniquities of image making because, in all the long history of political image making in Canada, there is nothing to compare with a trip from Ottawa to Hong Kong at public expense to be photographed signing a treaty with the Chinese communists which had, in fact, been signed two days before. I agree that there was a great deal for him in his position; but image making techniques can go too far. They are rather an unfortunate development on the body politic, and I am very glad indeed that this particular film was

Interim Supply
initiated by the C.B.C. and not by anyone connected with a government or with a political party.
The C.B.C. spokesmen, Mr. Chairman, stated from the beginning that they were anxious to film-and these are their words- "an intimate, candid, documentary study" of myself and the working of my office. They wanted to film conferences between myself and the ministers, as Mr. Ross McLean mentioned in his letter, and staff meetings, activities at my home and that sort of thing. They said they wanted to break new ground and produce an entirely new kind of t.v. film, and I think they succeeded.
After the clippings were done.

They emphasized that no similar film had ever been attempted by them and that new procedures and new arrangements for review would therefore be necessary in a film of this kind. This was the proposal made by the C.B.C.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I still hesitated. I was conscious that this might be a difficult, indeed an impossible operation, for a government corporation, and I don't mind admitting that I wish my hesitation had been more prolonged and had resulted in a negative decision. But it was emphasized again, to remove this hesitation, that for obvious reasons we would have to have the right, the customary right in pictures of this kind, the right of review of certain material to protect privacy because of the nature of the filming going on, to ensure good taste and the security of private conversations on questions of public policy.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I still had doubts even after these assurances, even after the filming began, so the producer, Mr. Ballen-tine, sent a letter to me on September 23 to remove these doubts and make it possible for him to go ahead with the production. We had every right to assume that this letter was sent with the knowledge and the approval of the C.B.C., because he was doing the job for them.
This letter is dated September 23, 1963 and it begins, "Dear Mr. Prime Minister" and includes these paragraphs:
I know that there is much we would like to film that you do not wish in the final documentary and the time you take to consider these requests is valuable. I can see that we are an embarrassment to you when you are with other people. I know of no way to eliminate these and the other problems entirely, but we can keep them to a minimum.

This is a paragraph which has already been referred to in the press and which I should put in, in its textual form, because it is extremely important. It gets to the heart of the arrangements made with regard to the film, and Mr. Ballentine writes as follows:
The finished film will be yours to judge and approve before it is made public and, thus, will contain nothing to which you object.
Now, that is a perfectly obvious arrangement to make because of the nature of the filming that was going on in my own home and outside the house. Mr. Ballentine further wrote:
But in this kind of film, candid documentary, we need access to a wealth of material in order to catch the right material. One of the great limitations of the camera is that, unlike a writer, if it isn't present it can never know what happened.
Then he went on and said this:
We would, however, appreciate being with you during as many private times as you can allow, so that we can begin filming again when you permit.
Because I had for the time being suspended operations.
In any event, anything we get on film that you have reservations about can be corrected later.

The fact that something is filmed does not compromise you or your staff in any way.
It was an effort on his part to remove my feeling that there would be a great deal of personal filming done. Indeed, that was insisted upon by the producer, that I must have some right of review in the interests of public security, and in case any secret conversations on policy were filmed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What secret conversations could you have as a member of the privy council?

I would be very glad to answer that question. There were conversations in my office with cabinet ministers and we talked about public policy. The cameraman wanted to have a film of this kind of operation going on, and it would be quite improper for a conversation between the Prime Minister and a minister to be filmed if it had dealt with some matter that had not been presented before the House of Commons; and we were anxious to make sure that would not happen in any public production.
Now, the film was subsequently discussed at its various stages, when we discussed it at all, with the C.B.C. and the producer on the basis of this agreement contained in a letter to me by the producer. But it was discussed with a full awareness on our part that there was need to respect the producer's editorial prerogative as well. The problem was to reconcile these two things. There was no transgression of editorial independence by our side and there was no request made either at that time or later by any member of the government or any representative of my office, or of mine, that the film in the form in which it was completed should be shown or not shown publicly. Never at any time was a request made that it be shown or not be shown. I make that statement as a member of this house and as leader of the government, and any insinuations to the contrary are false. And insinuations have been made in this house. Indeed, it has been charged in the house that we stopped the showing of this film. That charge is false.
Like your other statements.

Hear, hear.

Will the right hon. gentleman contain himself for a few moments and control his impatience. He will have his opportunity to speak and I am sure we will listen with interest to his remarks. In the meantime, let him keep silent.
Mr. Chairman, this is the second time in a week that the right hon. gentleman has talked about gutters. I wonder why he is always talking about gutters.
You should know.
The reason must be that I sit so close to the opposition.

I wish the right hon. gentleman would not single me out like this. It makes me nervous.

I rise on a point of order concerning the quotations made by the Prime Minister not only from the letter he is reading now but the letter he read a moment or two ago. I refer Your Honour to pages 328 and 329 of May's thirteenth edition where it is set forth that as a principle of debate a minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or state paper not before the house unless he is prepared to lay it on the table. This is also referred to by Beauchesne in citation 159. To go further, I should like to quote from Sir Gilbert Campion's book, "Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons" where the following words appear at page 195:
The rule as laid down by May (p. 433) is, "A minister is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he is prepared to lay it upon the table."
He is.
If hon. members opposite will wait for a while, they will see the point. They are always so anxious to impose closure here-
Oh, oh.

The citation continues:
The rule is akin to the rule of evidence in courts of law, and is a recognized standard for ministerial practice. It only applies to direct quotation from a paper, not to a mere summary of arguments contained. Nor is it always enforceable in the case of actual quotation. In the first place it may be overridden by considerations affecting the

public interest. Nor does it apply to private memoranda or correspondence or generally to any papers the production of which would, but for it, be refused to the house as being beyond its jurisdiction. The conclusion from these divergent considerations is that papers which cannot be laid in toto should not be read or quoted in extracts.
I submit that having regard to the number of times this matter has been raised in the house, and because they concern a matter of public importance, that these papers, or any others from which the Prime Minister attempts to quote should be laid on the table of the house in order that all members, and the country at large, may have all the facts which the Prime Minister is urgently attempting, he says, to lay before us.

Perhaps I may say a word on a point of order raised by the hon. member for Yukon. A similar point of order was raised previously when the Prime Minister was quoting from these letters. At that time you made a ruling, Mr. Chairman, to the effect that there was no obligation on the part of a minister, including the Prime Minister, to lay on the table any paper which was not a state paper. This is certainly not a state paper. You have made your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and it seems to me there is no validity in the point of order raised by the hon. member, particularly in view of the assurance given by the Prime Minister that he would consult with his correspondents, and that, with their permission, he would place on the table voluntarily the letters from which he is quoting.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Yukon has already spoken on this point of order. Does he wish to submit additional views?

Very briefly, Your Honour. I would simply point out in rebuttal of the Minister of Labour that the volume from which I quoted-the volume written by Sir Gilbert Campion-contains, in addition, this illuminating quotation:
Nor is it always enforceable in the case of actual quotations. In the first place it may be overridden by considerations affecting the public interest.
I submit that this issue is of overriding public interest, and because of this fact the Prime Minister should want to facilitate the placing of all the facts before the committee. He can only do this, surely, if he tables the documents from which he is quoting.

I simply rise on what I hope is a point of order to make a suggestion to the members of this house. It is this. In view

of the interest in this matter, which has been the subject of discussion for many days, and perhaps for the sake of the dignity and decorum of parliament, we might give the Prime Minister the privilege of being allowed to make his statement uninterrupted, and if we are not satisfied with what he has to say, then we have the opportunity on this supply motion to go after him.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A cursory look at the sixteenth edition of May confirms the position I took earlier when this point of order was first raised. If the hon. member would look at page 460 of that volume, he would see the following:
A minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table.
The word "state", of course, constitutes the distinction which must be drawn here. Then there is the following paragraph which appears at page 461:
A minister who summarizes a correspondence, but does not actually quote from it, is not bound to lay it upon the table. The rule for the laying of cited documents cannot be held to apply to private letters or memoranda.
Then it continues:
Indeed, it is obvious that, as the house deals only with public documents in its proceedings, it could not thus incidentally require the production of papers which, if moved for separately, would be refused as beyond its jurisdiction.
In other words, if the document is an official document the hon. member can move for its production. If it is not official, it does not have to be tabled if the Prime Minister, in this case, does not want to table it.
I might also refer the hon. member to citation 159(3) of Beauchesne's fourth edition:
It has been admitted that a document which has been cited ought to be laid upon the table of the house, if it can be done without injury to the public interest. The same rule, however, cannot be held to apply to private letters or memoranda. On the 18th May, 1865, the attorney general, on being asked by Mr. Ferrard if he would lay upon the table a written statement and a letter to which he had referred on a previous day, in answering a question relative to the Leeds bankruptcy court, replied that he had made a statement to the house upon his own responsibility, and that the documents he had referred to being private, he could not lay them upon the table. Lord Robert Cecil contended that the papers, having been cited, should be produced; but the Speaker declared that this rule applied to public documents only.

If I may continue, after the arrangements suggested to us by the C.B.C. were found acceptable and we agreed to proceed with the film, I must say that I lived not for one day but for a great many days under the eyes of a camera and tape recorder, as was the arrangement we made with those producing the film. It certainly was a candid camera. I lived and talked normally when the tape recorder and the camera were on hand, as did those with whom I was meeting. All this, Mr. Chairman was, of course, on the understanding that the interview filming or the actuality filming or the candid camera filming would produce a great deal of raw material from which anything within the category agreed upon for revisionary suggestions would be excluded in putting together the actual film as it was finally shown the press, and which I repeat I have never seen, myself- which deals, I hope with another point raised by the hon. member for Bow River.
I assumed from the beginning, Mr. Chairman, not having been told otherwise, that the film was being produced by the C.B.C. But we discovered as the filming went on that the nature of the working agreement between the C.B.C. and Intervideo Productions was such that the latter were in fact the actual producers, as agents for the C.B.C.
I was invited, Mr. Chairman, in accord with the arrangements made with the producer in my office, and to which I have referred in the letter, to see the first assembled version of the film, the first draft, on December 26 in Toronto, where I had been spending Christmas. And I did see that first draft; I said that in the house. That was not the film as it was finally produced and shown to the press.
Oh, oh.

It was not the film; it was the first draft. I have never seen the final draft. It is apparently on that distinction between the first draft, which I saw and which was greatly changed, and the final draft, which I did not see, that the hon. member for Bow River based his charge that I should resign, and I am sorry to disappoint him once again.
As a result of seeing the rough first draft in Toronto, Mr. Chairman, I asked a member

of my staff, in accordance with the arrangements suggested to us by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to bring to the attention of the producer certain sequences and tape recorded remarks which, in my view, were inappropriate and should be revised. They were in the categories for revision agreed upon. They were inappropriate because they were too personal, and there were one or two others which referred, in conversations with ministers, to matters which I thought should not be made public. They were under discussion, for one thing, in the House of Commons at that time. We were told by the producer for the C.B.C., we thought, that consideration would, of course, be given to these suggestions.
There was then a second review of the film in Ottawa, which was seen by members of my staff but not by me, a short time later, some time in January. Certain of the deletions which I had brought to the attention of the producer had been made; other deletions had not been made. The ones which had not been made included one which was a jocular and very personal remark made to me by Mrs. Pearson, who indeed did not realize when she made the remark that she was being filmed. It was a very personal remark. Second, there was a conversation with the Minister of Labour about the longshoremen's strike which was held in my office, and which I thought should not have been shown in the film. We had asked that this be taken out in the first instance, but it was not taken out of the second draft. Third, there was a reference to the Leader of the Opposition by the Clerk of the Privy Council. Mr. Robertson's comment was perfectly proper and entirely respectful in its mention of the Leader of the Opposition; but because it did mention the Leader of the Opposition by name I considered it to be an example of the type of remark and discussion taking place on a confidential basis which should be subject to revision and control, and which should not be included in the film; and that was not taken out.
These matters were brought to the attention of the C.B.C. and they were asked to reconsider the first suggestion that they should be excluded. They thought that this could be done at the time, and I was assured in January that there would be no special difficulty in meeting these suggestions, which were recognized to be, as I thought, quite reasonable.
There was a viewing of another revision of the film on January 21 in an office in

the east block. This was not the film as later
shown, but another revision. I saw part of this edition. It was the last version of the film I saw, and I saw only a small part of it because the sound and projection facilities were very bad. I also had to leave because I was going to Washington that afternoon to meet the President of the United States. I saw, however, 10 or 15 minutes of that version of the film. I learned when I got back that certain of the changes originally promised had, on the basis of that showing of the film, not yet been made.
On January 28 the director of the C.B.C. in charge of talks and programs of this kind wrote me, and again, Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to ask him to allow this letter to be tabled. The director asked me to agree that the arrangements proposed by Mr. Ballentine in his letter of September 23, and agreed to by me as the basis on which this production would proceed, be now set aside and that the program be completed in accordance with the normal principles and practices of the C.B.C. However, in his letter he added that they and the C.B.C. always bore in mind that I was fully entitled to raise objections to matters appearing in the program that touch on your private life or involve incidents or conversations normally and properly regarded as secret. I did not object to that proposal made by the representative of the C.B.C. but I replied that before any formal decision could be made by me there should be a further clarification of the relations between the corporation and Mr. Ballentine, which we had learned were becoming difficult, and we wished to know how this matter stood in regard to that relationship. The C.B.C. accepted that position.
Then later, Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. advised my office that they were anxious for us to see a print, as they put it, of the complete film. That was arranged for April 30, with three ministers and certain members of my office present. I was not there myself; I was not able to see that showing.
Who were the ministers?
Mr. Martin, Mr. Sharp and Mr. MacEachen.
