That is an episode which will live long in the history of parliamentary relations with the C.B.C. On the same day, May 20, the vice president of the C.B.C. released the following statement. This is the official statement of the C.B.C. and it should, of course, be put on the record in its entirety, though it is well known, I am sure, to hon. members. This is the statement issued in Toronto on May 20, 1964:
The C.B.C. has decided not to broadcast a filmed television program on a day in the life of the Prime Minister, entitled "Mr. Pearson-the Man and the Office".
The program was filmed for the corporation by Intervideo Productions Limited of Toronto.
C.B.C. senior program officials in Toronto viewed the finished print May 5, shortly after it became available to them, and decided it was unacceptable for broadcast, a decision concurred in by the program council and other senior executives.
It is the corporation's decision that the film does not meet C.B.C. program standards. The camera work is distracting: the lighting and sound are

Interim Supply
of uneven quality and often poor, and the editing is inadequate. These shortcomings are further aggravated by the problem of timeliness in some of the program content. The corporation recognizes it may have set a difficult objective for the film production and accepts its share of responsibility in this matter.
But there can be no sharing of decisions on what is broadcast or not broadcast. This is the corporation's responsibility. The program will not be broadcast because it does not meet minimum C.B.C. standards.
That was the formal decision made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Hon. gentlemen may challenge that decision if they will, but there is a decision in black and white. If the C.B.C. is to have a position of independence and prestige, which its importance deserves in this country, surely it is not helping the C.B.C. to challenge the validity and accuracy of a statement issued formally by them in respect of such an important matter.
Hear, hear.

In view of the discussions that have taken place, the charges that have been made and the insinuations that have been levelled, the C.B.C. is now referring the matter to its board of directors, who have met or are meeting. They are being given, as a board of directors, an opportunity to examine, presumably, the whole matter. I am speaking as a private member of this house, and though I know the risk involved in any kind of interference in this matter, in view of what has happened and in spite of the risk which may be entailed, I hope that the board of directors of the C.B.C. decide that in the circumstances this film should be shown to the Canadian public. If they make that decision, it will be their decision. If this film is shown I hope, Mr. Chairman, that this will be the end of the matter and we can get on with the business of legislation in this house.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the longer the Prime Minister spoke, the deeper became the mystery connected with the non-production of this film and the clearer it became that censorship was applied by the government or representatives of the Prime Minister. And let that be understood to begin with, because it is underlined everywhere.
I am going to deal with one of the meetings that he did not deal with; I shall do that a little later on. I am going to review some of the matters that he did not deal with, and understandably so. Censorship has been defined-and I take the dictionary defi-

nition here-as "control over; making excisions or changes". If ever there was a document that received the full treatment, the life of the Prime Minister as it was reviewed by Mr. Ballentine, by picture and voice, was such a document; but the Prime Minister and those associated with him did not desire it to be seen by the Canadian people.
As the Prime Minister spoke I could only conclude this; removing the smokescreens of personalities that punctuated his remarks, the Prime Minister is in the most difficult and trying position he has ever been in. He is embarrassed by his friends, embarrassed by his staff, embarrassed by his fellow members in the cabinet-and he is embarrassed because the facts finally came out when Mr. Ballentine revealed them. He said: Let us get on with the business of parliament. There is nothing more important, than that this house should assure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall not be a toy to be played with by the government of the day. The Prime Minister allowed this matter to drag on for two weeks before making a statement. He dealt very uncertainly with the contradictions and evasions pointed out by the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Yukon. He glossed over the fact that he had in fact seen the film in question. He says now that it was not the same one that exists today. It was one of the earlier ones before the operations took place thereon.
Sir, his statement today was, to anyone listening to it objectively, one that constituted an admission of a series of things that are inconsistent with any other hypothesis than that the government did not like the image in "Mr. Pearson". That is very clear.
I am going to deal in particular with the various events that took place right from the beginning. There is a strange situation here. The Prime Minister admits that there was an arrangement made with Mr. Ballentine whereby the Prime Minister or somebody associated with him would have a right of veto over the material produced. Cromwell once said: "Paint me, warts and all". In their several meetings the present government said in effect: Paint me, but put nothing in that will in any way deteriorate the image that Madison avenue has endeavoured to create.
Sir, there were veto rights. The Prime Minister says that the reason for the veto rights was so that matters of secrecy would not be made available to the Canadian people. I ask, why were matters of secrecy being discussed between the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet knowing that

not only were photographers and technicians present but that a record was being made? Surely that is a strange explanation. Certainly there should be no revelation of secrets, but why make them available by discussing such matters in the presence of these people?
The Prime Minister would brush this matter aside and say that there is really nothing to it. He would have us believe that it is a trivial situation and that parliament should not be wasting its time on it. I say immediately that censorship is clearly apparent, that interference with the C.B.C. was revealed by him in his remarks and that it is quite apparent that the reason for the suppression was the fact that the high officials of the C.B.C. realized that, to say the least, the government was not pleased with the production that was made.
What has been done here strikes at the very roots of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If I had time I should like to quote what the Minister of Transport said on one occasion. In this case the C.B.C. has allowed itself to become the government's cat's-paw because the Prime Minister and those associated with him did not like what they saw. He said that the deletions were in the interests of security. I ask him, whose security was affected when these various words of pseudo-profanity were removed? What security was affected when the deity was reduced from four to one in mentions by the Prime Minister? Surely such nonsense as he endeavoured to place before us today is answered as one goes into detail regarding the several meetings that took place.
No censorship? What were the ministers there for? It must have been a most enjoyable film because there were 12 reviews. I have seen people go to the movies for the first show and stay for the second because they enjoyed the picture, but for one or other of these five ministers to see this film in its several repetitions is something else again. Was it because of the entertainment value? Were they there purely and simply for the purpose of trying to understand the nature of the picture and to recommend excisions that were based on secrecy? What they were trying to do was to bury something that they did not want seen by the Canadian people.
The facts would never have come out, Mr. Chairman, if it had not been for the revelations made in two Toronto newspapers. We know the facts and there has been no denial. I want to review these various meetings because there is one in particular to which

reference has not been made. Throughout the Prime Minister's speech Keith Davey was present in the diplomatic gallery, which is an indication that he has a diplomatic interest in the discussions that are taking place on this occasion. Why his interest? Why his presence on the 5th day of April? Why the presence of these other ministers? Why these various screenings?
I think we ought to review first some of the screenings because they reveal a most interesting situation. The first of the political screenings took place in December. The Prime Minister's press secretary was there and also his appointments secretary, Mr. Coutts, who I am informed has emerged as a promising candidate for Hollywood, and the only one who did. Mr. O'Hagan was also there on that occasion, December 23, I believe. They were worried about sequences. I am not going into the particulars. There was worry about the Coutts car sequence. That had nothing to do with secrecy. It was a revelation, I understand, but it had nothing to do with secrecy.
On the 26th of December, Boxing day, again they gathered and there were present the assistant press secretary, James Reagan, the Minister of Finance, who is quite a judge of the aesthetic although I understand he just happened to walk in on the thing and was not really a party to the gathering, and the Prime Minister. We are informed that what the Minister of Finance saw regarding the Prime Minister did not fill that minister with the assurance and feeling that it should be reproduced.
Then things started to move. The Prime Minister endeavoured to have the house believe that there was no interference, no censorship. Why all these meetings? On January 6, 1964 another meeting was held at the request of Mr. O'Hagan, the press secretary of the Prime Minister, and there they really got the scissors out. There, they really pointed out what should be removed. They asked that a remark by Mr. O'Hagan about the Canadian Press, a remark by the right hon. gentleman about a former press secretary of the opposition leader, an unguarded remark by the Minister of Labour, a facetious remark by a lady, comments by the government chauffeur, be removed. On that occasion there was no censorship. It was said that there were rather too many references to the deity. They finally decided that one reference would be enough and the rest would go by the board. Was that in the interests of security?

Well, I would have liked to hear the remarks by the chauffeur, because they certainly could not have done anything. Then, there was a further one by Mr. O'Hagan. Did you ever see such anxiety on the part of a prime minister and those associated with him to see something that they were not going to interfere with? They just came to see, to listen. I hear the Prime Minister walked out on one showing because he said the tonal effects were such that he could not understand himself. I can only say, in the kindest way, that we have been in the same position this afternoon.
On January 21, there was a screening for the Prime Minister, but he walked out. He had to go somewhere, and I understand that. Following that, there were requests for more deletions. Sir, when the Prime Minister says, "We do not censor films on this side of the house", I wonder what it is. Was it an exercise in self-appreciation? Did they want to see themselves as others see them? Did something there not appeal to their finer, aesthetic sensibilities? Why these repeated showings?
On this occasion, there were a number of things, I think, that went out. One was the reference by the Clerk of the Privy Council to the Leader of the Opposition; one was the Coutts car sequence and the final deity was taken out altogether. You see, they are making progress. You can just see them, Mr. Chairman. There they sit.
I will come now to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who had a notebook. We wish he were here. Then, there was the screening on April 5 in the east block. I should like to have been present in that cave of Adullam, when all of these disgruntled people got together. The Prime Minister said he would not give me the names because he was not going to mention his staff. I do not want to know about his staff. I do not want him to have to defend his staff. They were simply carrying out their responsibilities under his direction. There was no screening in his office. It must have been a great get-together over there, just like the beginning of a premiere. There was everything except the searchlights and the autograph hunters.
Who was present? There was the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I don't know whether he was trying to find markets abroad for it. There was the Secretary of State for External Affairs and Mr. Tom Kent. Of course, he is on the Prime Minister's staff. However, Keith Davey was not on the staff.

What was he doing there? He was present on that occasion and he was in the diplomatic gallery today. What was he there for? I am sure it was not for the purpose in any way, according to the Prime Minister, of censorship. He was just there to enjoy himself. I hope he enjoyed himself more than the Prime Minister has since. Here was the whole office staff of image makers gathered together with their wives and secretaries.
Then, the Secretary of State for External Affairs decided that he had to do something in the interests of the observation of the international amenities. He looked the thing over, and he said: I object to these points. He said it conjured up in him feelings of regret, that there had been some mistake made. There were no politics in there, no censorship, but imagine a picture in which there were two particular views of Macdonald and none of Laurier. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that was not proper. Then, Emperor Haile Selassie came into it. Somebody said, is he the only emperor in the world today? I am informed that the Prime Minister said-this is all hearsay and if he says it did not take place I will immediately withdraw it with apologies-[DOT] "I think there is another emperor in Cambodia; you cannot keep up with these things''. They forgot altogether about the emperor of Japan, so out went any reference to Haile Selassie in the form in which it originated. This was an amazing performance.
There was a discussion of profanity, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs was worried about the effect of that language on Presbyterians and Methodists. Mr. Chairman, it would be ridiculous in any forum; but this is a serious effort on the part of the Prime Minister and his cabinet, facing great issues in Canada, and they are worrying about the use of words that are in general use within our country. Then it is said, and again if the Minister of Labour says it did not take place I will accept his word, that the Minister of Labour has a discerning taste for things aesthetic. He was not shocked by what he saw. He said it was highly amusing. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said it was an astounding document. Apparently they did not have agreement in cabinet that day, because to others that which was astounding and amazing was neither.
Now, that is just a short record. I could place a great deal more on the record were I to choose to do so but I do not want to bring up anything further in this connection because my time is disappearing. But I do

say this to the Prime Minister on the basis of what he said today, that while his words denied censorship what he said admitted censorship in every sense of the word. I said a moment ago I was not going to quote the Minister of Transport, but I think I should. This is what he said on January 18:
I may say that I fully subscribe to that view and X have, I think, In my private life and in my public life always been a supporter of public broadcasting for that reason, and for that reason only, because I do recognize the dangers of public broadcasting as they were manifest in some parts of Europe 25 years ago when some of us were rather younger than we are now, and as they still exist today in many totalitarian countries. This is potentially a very dangerous instrument in the hands of an unscrupulous government and it needs to be safeguarded in every possible way against control by the government as opposed to control by parliament itself in which people are freely elected whether or not the people who elect them like the government.
Sir, can anyone deny that the 12 showings were held, the multiplicity of showings, without the government having pointed out that they did not like what they saw? They admitted they tore it asunder. They did not remove-no; they asked, they suggested, they publicly stated in these meetings what they saw wrong in what was taking place.
Sir, it is a picture that is hard to understand. The Prime Minister said he did not have anything to do with it, that it was not he who asked to see it. I point out that on December 24 Mr. McLean of the C.B.C. had a request from the Prime Minister to see the film and it was stated he could see the film on Boxing day. Sir, all the way along, all through the piece, the Prime Minister was there examining, either in his own person or through the means of those of his staff. He cannot get away from that.
Why was it cancelled out? Well now, just a nod from the government might have its effect, but a continuing campaign of 12 meetings of condemnation and of suggestion could not leave the C.B.C. in any other position than, to use the immortal words of the Secretary of State, "heads might roll".
Why all these meetings? On May 7, after all these peregrinations back and forth, in Toronto, in Ottawa, in the various locations here, Mr. Ballentine wrote a letter to Mr. Alphonse Ouimet and asked about this and he received a letter, according to what he says, simply reading "Mr. Ballentine"-without "Yours truly" even added, stating the film did not meet with C.B.C. programming standards, that the camera work was distracting and that the quality of editing was inadequate. They did not find this out until

ministers gathered together over and over again and looked upon what they saw, and were not pleased.
Sir, why was this stopped? On May 5 Mr. Ballentine was called into Mr. Haggan's office-and a more reputable man there is not anywhere to be found-and told the telecast had been scheduled for June 25. Later that day the final decision was made that it be not shown, and later on Mr. Haggan telephoned Mr. Ballentine and said he wanted to screen it one last time for his superiors, one last screening after all the screenings, and the screenings, and the screenings, and the screenings multiplied several times.
They had this screening in Toronto, attended by the top C.B.C. programming people, and at nine o'clock that night Mr. Haggan telephoned Mr. Ballentine and said the program officials in Toronto and Ottawa had decided not to have the film run. If ever there was a flagrant interference with the C.B.C. this is one, and all the Prime Minister does is endeavour to bring along a number of smokescreens. He did not answer this. He gave no explanation whatever regarding all these interesting revelations that were being made.
He told us today that any excisions were to be made on the basis of security. I ask this again as I did earlier, whose security? As I look at the government opposite and I see them as they join together, the security that they had in mind, as they interpreted the national security, was their own political security and nothing else.
From beginning to end the story is one that is now worse than it was following the explanation of the Prime Minister. Why did he have the head of his national Liberal organization present? Was that in order to assure security? I would like to have an answer to that. He talked today about calculated malevolence. Bringing forth the facts is not malevolence, but the discharge of constitutional responsibility. It is always the case that when people find themselves in a serious position, as he and those associated with him do, they resort to that type of personal abuse that was levied against the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Yukon.
Sir, I could say a great deal more but I simply set out in very terse detail the sinuous course taken by this government, and it got found out.
The Prime Minister said no pictures were taken in the cabinet. Well, all I have to say is that I would like to have this matter brought before a committee of parliament

and Mr. Ballentine given the opportunity to give evidence. I must accept what the Prime Minister says, but Mr. Ballentine says it took place.
Mr. Ballentine, if he is correctly reported has said:
Shooting now continued in Ottawa, at the Prime Minister's home, in his office, in his private limousine as he drove to the east block, at a meeting of the cabinet in the privy council chamber.
This last occasion was on the day after the Ontario election and all members of the cabinet spoke for about 15 minutes on the political implications of that event.
It will be recalled that one or other of the ministers took a prominent part in that connection, and it was on that occasion the pictures were taken, according to Mr. Ballentine.
Later that day Mr. Pearson asked Mr. Ballentine not to use the cabinet sequence since his colleagues were shocked at the idea of their remarks being recorded for television. The producer assented.
If Mr. Ballentine is correctly reported, then all I can say is that I am surprised he would not know the difference between four or five ministers in the Prime Minister's office in the east block, and a whole lot of ministers in the privy council office. But that is not what the Prime Minister says, and I would like to hear the views of Mr. Ballentine in this connection. In order to get to the bottom of this and get the facts we have to have his story and know what has taken place.
Now I pass on for a moment and I refer to what happened on June 18. In this city a group of young men known as the Confederation club announced they were going to show something of what had taken place by revealing the particular print that they had. So far as the film negative is concerned it is held in escrow in Toronto by Pathe News, or some of those organizations.
Who interfered on this occasion? Was Mr. Ballentine advised that he would not be allowed to do this? Was he told he would be refused permission to use the film that belonged to him? Why was that done? Is it not further evidence of the suppression that is characteristic throughout the entire period of this continuing performance? It was not 60 days of decision; it was eight months of indecision. I think that is the number of months that it was before one group or another. It started in September. It went on for several weeks. The climax was on October 7, the day the Prime Minister had the pictures taken in his office. What happened in all those months? Why the change? Why was it that

for the first time, late in May, the order was given that this film was not to be produced?
Now what about it? The Canadian people have a right to see, not the expurgated edition, not the excised edition, not the edition to which scissors under the direction of ministers have been taken; the Canadian people have the right to see this film as it was originally produced, before so much of it found its way on to the cutting floor. What has taken place here is a serious act of censorship.
I cannot understand it. Last evening, on the national television network, the C.B.C., there was not one reference to what took place yesterday. Not a word. Why? Why was there nothing in this regard? What took place is just as serious as censoring a newspaper article of which one does not approve. Indeed, it is immeasurably worse, because this is a government corporation. Do you mean to tell me, sir, that the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister and the members of the Prime Minister's staff and Keith Davey are able to fill the positions of producers and directors, adding here, snipping there, chopping somewhere else-all for artistic considerations or for security purposes? That is what the Prime Minister said. I do not intend to quote what the Minister of Finance was alleged to have said. But I can imagine what happened in the C.B.C. when word came to them: "Paul does not like it." I can just see the fluttering of the dovecots as they began to realize that the Secretary of State for External Affairs thought something was wrong.
Be that as it may, this film should be restored, and what the image makers tore asunder should be replaced and put together. To do otherwise, to produce what has been revised, to produce what has gone through the hopper of governmental disinfection, is not what we are entitled to expect. What we are entitled to see is the film which was originally produced, subject to one consideration-that if there is anything at all affecting national security, no one would ask that it be produced.
On the other hand, what decisions, what legislation, what planning on the part of the Prime Minister and cabinet ministers could possibly justify the discussion of security matters in these circumstances, whether in the cabinet room or in the Prime Minister's office?
Hear, hear.

That was one of the most serious revelations made this afternoon. I can understand the Prime Minister's feelings in this situation. All of us have a great deal more hindsight than we have foresight. He laid the foundations for what he wanted. The private secretaries, the executive secretaries and the president or the chairman of the national organization had their ideas. The C.B.C. made a mistake when it accepted the veto right of anyone in that agreement which was entered into and accepted by the Prime Minister. I should like to see the letter which was written to him by Mr. Ballentine in that connection or on his behalf.
The picture was produced. I can just see them. How they must have enjoyed it. They asked: Show it over and over again; give it to us again. And every time they looked at it they had a few more qualifications to make, a few more subtractions, a few more diminutions. Finally, even what was then produced did not meet with the high standards of the government. They saw much wrong in it; they saw things in it which were detrimental to the national security-which I define as being the political security of the Liberal party, translated into higher spheres by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
There has not been a more serious matter before parliament than this. Now the board of governors is meeting. What a dish of crow has been handed to them. Mr. Ouimet says there has been no improvement in the technical qualifications of the film. Yet now, because, as he said, there are larger matters to be considered, he has placed this question before the board. These are his words:
The corporation must at all times be careful not to confuse political matters with questions of broadcast responsibility.

That is what this government put the corporation in the position of doing. With respect to the present situation it does not appear to the corporation that parliament has clearly indicated a view.
Then he says this:
The corporation has already taken a broadcast decision with respect to this film. That decision was based solely on the professional broadcasting standards of the corporation which are used to judge such matters. The film has not changed and the standards have not changed.
I accept that statement. Then I ask: What were you people doing there? What were you doing there with this great coterie and retinue, with all the staff surrounding you? I end with these words from the quotation:
Consequently, the corporation must determine whether more compelling factors now exist in the realm of the public interest.
What are the more compelling factors? The most compelling up to date has been the interference on the part of this government. What is more compelling than that?
May I raise one point in connection with the tabling of the letters?
